topic.title: What if the Panama Canal ran out of water?
topic.map_answer: the lake in the middle of the isthmus that every ship crosses, shrinking on the map as the rain stops, and the long detour route drawn round the bottom of South America when it can no longer be crossed

title: Why can't the Panama Canal work without rain?
description:
The Panama Canal, the shortcut between two oceans, depends on a lake, and the lake depends on rain.
What happens to the world's ships if the rain stops, on the map.
Sources: MAX Security, IMF (Dec 2023). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Rain or ships: which does Panama need more? Comment

lines.text: Without rain, the Panama Canal stops.
So what if it never rained there again?
It nearly happened. In a drought, the canal cut the ships crossing each day from 36 to just 22.
Why would a canal need rain? It isn't a flat ditch from sea to sea. Ships climb up into a lake in the middle of Panama, Gatun Lake, then step back down to the other ocean.
And where does the water go? Every ship that crosses lets a huge gulp of the lake's fresh water run out into the sea.
The only thing that fills it back up is rain, falling on the forest all around it.
So if the rain stops for good, the lake sinks a little with every ship, the locks run short, and fewer and fewer ships get through.
At both ends, the line of waiting ships grows longer every day, each one loaded with cargo that someone, somewhere, is waiting for.

Until the only way left is the long way round: all the way down South America, round stormy Cape Horn, and back up the other side. Weeks at sea, instead of about half a day going straight through the canal.
And about 5% of all the world's trade by sea goes through this one canal: cars, grain and fuel. All of it riding on the rain.
Rain or ships: which does Panama need more? Tell me. Because without rain,

Facts confirmed: 5% of global maritime trade on the IMF page (15 Nov 2023); 22/day 2023-24 drought cap on the MAX Security page (late 2023), also gCaptain (Nov 2026) and Reuters (Aug 2026); 36/day normal confirmed by search (Reuters 'down from 36 ships in normal conditions', AP '36 to 38'), because the MAX page words it inconsistently ('36 vessels... in a month'). Story is still current: the 2026 El Nino cuts went only to 32 and were raised to 34 on 9 Nov 2026, so 22 is still the low. Lock and lake mechanics, freshwater lost per transit and rain refilling Gatun are correct. Description ends with the disclaimer. Notes: 'It nearly happened' slightly overstates a cut to 22 a day, and the Cape Horn detour simplifies (real 2023 diversions also used Suez/Good Hope or the Strait of Magellan); both acceptable in a what-if.

The 5% stays an IMF sourced fact.
